name: Authentication & Passwords
description: Password security, biometrics, multi-factor and passwordless authentication (FIDO/WebAuthn).

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from USENIX 2018, treat passwords as a stubborn fact of life and try to understand or patch their weaknesses rather than replace them. Several are empirical and human-centered: "Better managed than memorized? Studying the Impact of Managers on Password Strength and Reuse" (2018) and "Forgetting of Passwords: Ecological Theory and Data" (2018) probe how real users cope with memory and tooling, while "The Rewards and Costs of Stronger Passwords in a University" (2018) studies how an actual password policy plays out at scale. Alongside these sit early systems and protocol concerns — "Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (IoT)" (2018) reframes authentication for multi-user device settings, and "O Single Sign-Off, Where Art Thou?" (2018) exposes session and account-hijacking gaps in SSO. This year sets the tone: passwords are insecure but entrenched, so the work is about measuring damage and hardening the ecosystem.

By 2019-2020 the field pivots from individual passwords toward the broader account-protection ecosystem and toward biometrics as an alternative. "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) operationalizes breach data to defend accounts at scale, and "Birthday, Name and Bifacial-security" (2019) broadens the empirical lens beyond English-speaking users to Chinese passwords. At the same time, biometrics and liveness become central: "Void: A fast and light voice liveness detection system" (USENIX 2020) and "Liveness is Not Enough: Enhancing Fingerprint Authentication with Behavioral Biometrics to Defeat Puppet Attacks" (2020) show both the promise and the spoofing risks of biometric factors. Two-factor authentication also arrives as a serious object of study with "Empirical Measurement of Systemic 2FA Usability" (2020), shifting attention from whether 2FA is secure to whether organizations can actually live with it.

From 2021 to 2022 the work increasingly targets adoption, deployment, and the fragility of newer factors. "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (USENIX 2021) turns 2FA into a design and behavioral problem of nudging users, while "Inexpensive Brainwave Authentication" (2021) and "Card Brand Mixup Attack" (2021) explore exotic biometrics and break real payment-card authentication respectively. Deepfakes raise the stakes for biometric trust in "Seeing is Living? Rethinking the Security of Facial Liveness Verification in the Deepfake Era" (USENIX 2022), and email-authentication measurement matures with "A Large-scale and Longitudinal Measurement Study of DKIM Deployment" (2022).

Most recently, USENIX 2023 shows two clear fronts. On classic passwords, machine learning sharpens guessing attacks and evaluation — "Improving Real-world Password Guessing Attacks via Bi-directional Transformers" (2023), "Password Guessing Using Random Forest" (2023), and "Pass2Edit" (2023) model how users create and edit passwords, while "No Single Silver Bullet: Measuring the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (2023) audits the meters meant to guide users. On the ecosystem side, "A Study of Multi-Factor and Risk-Based Authentication Availability" (2023) measures how far real services have actually moved beyond plain passwords, and emerging interfaces draw scrutiny in "Hidden Reality: Caution, Your Hand Gesture Inputs in the Immersive Virtual World are Visible to All!" (2023). The arc runs from measuring password pain, to building account-protection and biometric defenses, to ML-driven attack/defense and broad measurement of whether multi-factor and risk-based authentication are reaching users.

top4.narrative:
The 2018 papers in this list show a field organized around two long-standing problems: making text passwords less brittle, and patching the systems built on top of them. On the password side, work focused on measuring and improving the basics, from auditing how well password strength meters actually predict resistance to cracking ("On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters," CCS 2018) to modeling the economics of an offline cracker ("On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking," S&P 2018) and even using fake "honeyword" decoys to detect breaches ("A Security Analysis of Honeywords," NDSS 2018). A parallel thread treated authentication as a systems problem: single sign-on session hijacking ("O Single Sign-Off, Where Art Thou?," USENIX 2018), local IPC attacks on security keys ("Man-in-the-Machine," USENIX 2018), and the human-factors reality that two-factor hardware is hard to use ("A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability," S&P 2018). Early biometric and side-channel work also appeared, from liveness detection ("Face Flashing," NDSS 2018) to inferring Android unlock patterns from sound ("PatternListener," CCS 2018).

The big shift in 2019 was the rise of credential reuse and breach-driven attacks as a first-class research target. Once billions of leaked passwords were public, the question became how to defend at scale, and a tight cluster of papers answered it: Google's breach-alerting deployment ("Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting," USENIX 2019), neural models that predict how attackers tweak a leaked password for a different site ("Beyond Credential Stuffing: Password Similarity Models Using Neural Networks," S&P 2019), and the cryptographic protocols ("Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials," CCS 2019) needed to check leaks without leaking. The same period broadened the lens beyond English speakers ("Birthday, Name and Bifacial-security," USENIX 2019) and pushed machine learning deeper into guessing, culminating in representation-learning attacks ("Improving Password Guessing via Representation Learning," S&P 2021).

Around 2020 the field began seriously imagining a world after passwords, while also confronting new sensors and form factors. "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?" (S&P 2020) put passwordless FIDO2/WebAuthn under a usability microscope, signaling that standards-based public-key authentication was finally deployable. At the same time, biometrics matured from a feature into an arms race: voice liveness detection ("Void," USENIX 2020), behavioral defenses against fingerprint puppet attacks ("Liveness is Not Enough," USENIX 2020), and adversarial attacks that fool speaker recognition outright ("Who is Real Bob?," S&P 2021). Empirical studies grounded mobile reality, quantifying how guessable smartphone PINs are ("This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed," S&P 2020) and giving deployable password-policy advice ("Practical Recommendations for Stronger, More Usable Passwords," CCS 2020).

Most recently the frontier has moved in two directions. First, authentication for emerging platforms, with AR/VR becoming its own subarea ("OcuLock," NDSS 2020; "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality," S&P 2022) and privacy-preserving biometrics on commodity hardware ("EchoHand," CCS 2022). Second, a cryptographic reimagining of identity itself, moving from "do I know your password" toward provable, privacy-preserving credentials: decentralized, Sybil-resistant identity ("CanDID," S&P 2021) and anonymous credentials built on zkSNARKs atop existing identity infrastructure ("zk-creds," S&P 2023). The throughline across these venues is a steady migration away from shared secrets toward cryptographic keys, liveness-aware biometrics, and verifiable-yet-private identity.
